author: John Steinbeck
introFa: کتاب «Of Mice and Men (Adapted Reader)» نوشته John Steinbeck یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح B1 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «Of Mice and Men (Adapted Reader)»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

Many epidemiological studies into NAT-related cancer susceptibility have been carried out3 and analysis of these combined studies is now possible. The role of NAT in predisposition to cancer depends on the type of cancer, the ethnicity of the population and probably also on the level of exposure to carcinogens. However, there is a consensus of opinion that the slow acetylator type represents a risk factor in bladder cancer3. The development of very large, multi-centre epidemiological studies will help to identify the role of NAT polymorphisms in a range of environmentally induced cancers6. Our current understanding of NATs has entered a new phase as a result of the availability of genome sequences and the first three-dimensional (3D) structure of a member of this unique family of enzymes. In this article, the major issues concerning NAT research at present will be discussed. Distribution of NATs NATs were first identified in human liver and intestinal epithelial cytosols7. In the early 1960s it was already clear that different classes of substrates are acetylated by distinct enzymes, which are present in both of these tissues. Such classes of substrates were designated as either polymorphic (e.g. isoniazid) or monomorphic (e.g. p-aminosalicylate)1. Since then, NATs and anti-bacterial agents have been inextricably linked and this inter-relationship has taken a new twist with the availability of genome sequences for many microorganisms. The existence of NAT homologues in bacteria has been predicted on the basis of homology searching (Fig. 1), and NATs have been characterized through cloning and expression of functional genes8. Although endogenous NAT activity has been detected in many bacterial strains (Ref. 9 and J-M. Du Pret et al., unpublished), this activity has not always been associated with the existence of a NAT- homologous sequence in completed genomes (e.g. in Helicobacter pylori10), suggesting that another group of enzymes might be involved. Of the bacterial NAT-like gene sequences that have been identified, those of mycobacteria, including Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the causative agent of tuberculosis11, are of particular interest. The expression of NAT in mycobacteria can influence the sensitivity of these organisms to the anti-tubercular agent isoniazid8 and therefore could influence resistance to isoniazid. Pigeons and chickens both exhibit NAT activity and, indeed, these birds played an important role in early understanding of NAT. For example, enzymological studies on pigeon liver led to the proposal of the ‘ping–pong’ nature of the NAT acetylation reaction with a short-lived acetyl intermediate proposed as being formed before transfer of the acetyl group to the arylamine substrate12. The chicken was the first organism from which NAT was cloned13. Mainly as a result of the studies of Weber and his colleagues, in an effort to develop models for understanding human acetylator polymorphism, inbred strains of many animals showing either fast or slow acetylator phenotype were established1. In rats, hamsters and mice, point mutations that result in single amino acid substitutions can affect the activities of NAT isoenzymes. In rats and hamsters there are two genes encoding NAT, one of which is polymorphic. Rabbits also have two genes but the slow acetylator type is associated with the loss of one of the two Nat genes14. Cats and other felids have a single Nat gene15. In all mammalian organisms that express a NAT gene, including cows16, the gene product shows a specificity for p-aminobenzoic acid (p-aba). In mice and humans the NAT isoenzyme that metabolizes p-aba also catalyses the acetylation of the folate break-down product p-aminobenzoylglutamate (p-ABglu) to convert it to the urinary folate metabolite p-N- acetamidobenzoylglutamate17. The widespread tissue distribution of the p-aba acetylating activity in hamsters, rats, mice, cats and humans has led to the suggestion that this isoenzyme is involved in endogenous metabolism. Acetylating the folate breakdown product is now generally accepted to be an endogenous role of this enzyme, although it has recently been suggested that NAT is involved in the maintenance of acetyl CoA homeostasis18. The lack of NAT in canids19 is thought to be due to inherent metabolic differences. The specificity profile of the NATs identified from bacteria and mycobacteria are more like human NAT2 in that they acetylate isoniazid and do not acetylate p-aba (Refs 8,9,20). This is not surprising given that bacteria synthesize folate de novo from p-aba. One member of the NAT family that has been identified in prokaryotes is the terminal enzyme in the rifamycin synthesis cluster in the gram-positive Amycolatopsis mediterranei21 and thus different NAT variants might perform a range of roles in different organisms in which they are found. Structural studies NAT from Salmonella typhimurium20 reached particular prominence when the strains that are particularly sensitive in the Ames mutagenesis assay were created through incorporation of the gene encoding O-acetyltransferase, which was also shown to code for NAT. Indeed, S. typhimurium has played a major role in unravelling the mechanism of action of NAT. Early inhibition and labelling studies with eukaryotic NATs initially implicated a cysteine residue as essential for NAT activity22. This cysteine was subsequently identified by sequence comparison of all NAT sequences available at that time as Cys69 in S. typhimurium NAT, which corresponds to Cys68 in most eukaryotic NATs. The identity of the essential cysteine was strengthened by the loss of activity when the proposed active-site cysteine was mutated to alanine in S. typhimurium NAT and also in human NAT2 (Refs 20,23,24). Recently, the 3D structure of NAT from S. typhimurium has been obtained, approximately eight years after the determination of its sequence25. This has revealed a structure that consists of three domains (Fig. 2a). The first domain (85 N-terminal amino acids) forms five α-helices, the second domain (residues 86–175) has eight strands of β-sheet, and the third C-terminal domain comprises four strands of β-sheet and a further two α-helices. Residues 176–202 form an inter-domain helical region. The crystal structure shows the active site Cys69 to be visible in a cleft between the first and second domains, situated in an active-site triad with His107 and Asp122. This catalytic triad is very reminiscent of the catalytic triad common to the cysteine protease family as has previously been discussed for NAT (Ref. 26). Sequence analysis of all known NATs shows these residues to be invariant. In addition, the recently solved crystal structure of NAT from Mycobacterium smegmatis also shows the catalytic triad. A fragment of human NAT1, now known to correspond to the first two domains and therefore to contain the residues of the proposed catalytic triad, has previously been shown to catalyse the first acetylation step from acetyl CoA but is unable to transfer the acetyl group to an arylamine27. These results suggest a universal reaction mechanism for NAT enzymes in which the catalytic triad is essential for the first step of the reaction but the third domain is the arylamine-binding site. Previous site-directed mutagenesis experiments on human NATs had implicated that a histidine residue was important in catalysis24. The 3D structure of NAT from S. typhimurium supports the role of His107 in acid–base catalysis. However, the arginine residues that were thought to participate in base catalysis20,24 now seem more likely to be involved in salt bridges, which maintain the required juxtaposition of the cysteine and histidine in the catalytic triad. Residues 125 and 127 of both human NATs were previously predicted to be important in activity and substrate specificity28. From the crystal structure of S. typhimurium NAT (see the region encompassing Gly126 in Fig. 2b), it would appear that these residues are likely to be close to the active site. However, such predictions can only be tested by the determination of the crystal structure of the human NATs themselves. Progress towards the structures of eukaryotic NATs has been made by the crystallization of hamster NAT2 (Ref. 29). Human NAT proteins The human NAT proteins, each 290 amino acids long, share 87% amino acid identity but possess different substrate-specificity profiles30. Substrates of NAT1 include p-aba, p-aminosalicylic acid31 and p-ABglu, a folate catabolite and possible endogenous substrate17. NAT1 might modulate the concentration of acetyl CoA (Ref. 18). Specific NAT2 substrates include the anti- tubercular drug isoniazid, and sulfamethazine. Human NAT1 transcripts have been detected in blastocysts (i.e. before neurulation in human development17), which is an intriguing finding in view of the role of human NAT1 in folate catabolism and the protective effect of folate in neural tube defects. However, the precise relationship between human NAT1 activity and protection from neural tube defects remains to be established. Human NAT loci Human NAT genes are located on chromosome 8p22 within a region of 140–360 kb (Ref. 34). There are three loci: NAT1 and NAT2 are functional genes, and NATP is a pseudogene35. Human NAT2 has a non- coding exon 8 kb upstream of its start codon36 but human NAT1 apparently does not35,37. The control of expression of these very similar intron-less coding regions requires further analysis. Both NAT1 and NAT2 are multi-allelic5. The frequency of the alleles, which depends on the ethnicity of the population (Table 1), accounts for the higher frequency of fast acetylators of NAT2 substrates in Japanese and Taiwanese populations (see http://www.louisville.edu/medschool/ pharmacology/NAT.html for details of alleles). The effect of polymorphisms on phenotype is well established for NAT2 (Ref. 3), although the molecular mechanism of ‘slow’ acetylation varies for different alleles. For NAT1, some point mutations in the coding region can be classified as reducing activity (Table 2) but the effect of mutations outside the coding region has been controversial. Early studies indicating an increase in activity associated with the NAT1*10 allele38 have not been supported in subsequent studies39–42. It appears that the NAT1*10 mutation within the putative polyadenylation site does not affect the level of NAT1 expression43. Many of the NAT alleles at both the NAT2 and the NAT1 loci are associated with mutation ‘hotspots’ and D8S21 (a polymorphic marker on human chromosome 8) has been sited in the NAT2 gene34. Linkage disequilibrium has been observed between NAT2*4 and NAT1*10 in Caucasian populations42,44 and the increased frequency of NAT1*10 in Oriental populations (Table 1) suggests that the same linkage exists in other ethnic groups. The recently completed sequence of the human genome allows the identification of microsatellite repeats within the vicinity of the NAT genes, which will be useful for longer-range linkage analysis. Murine NATs: models to determine the effects of polymorphism and gene expression To understand the role of NAT polymorphism in human disease susceptibility, mammalian models that demonstrate fast and slow acetylation types were established by Weber and colleagues1. Mouse models are now particularly useful because of the wealth of information available on murine development and transgenic technology. There are three murine Nat genes, Nat1, Nat2 and Nat3, each encoding a functional protein of 290 amino acids17. So far, only one gene, murine Nat2, shows polymorphism: a single-point mutation in which amino acid 99 is changed from asparagine to isoleucine, resulting in a ‘slow’ protein that is less stable than the rapid acetylator version45. Historically, this mouse gene was designated Nat2 because, like human NAT2, the protein that it encodes demonstrated polymorphism, and recently researchers working on NAT have decided to maintain this nomenclature5. However, for those not in the field, this could be confusing because it is now known that murine Nat2 encodes the functional equivalent of the human NAT1 isoenzyme. These two proteins have the same pattern of expression and substrate specificity, acetylating p-aba and p-ABglu (thought to reside in the similarities in the sequence of the C-terminal 14 amino acids). Murine NAT2, like human NAT1, is found in a wide range of tissues and is expressed early in development46,47. In view of their proposed role in folate catabolism, it might be important that the murine Nat2 gene is expressed, like human NAT1, before neurulation at the blastocyst stage, and also that the expressed protein can be detected immunohistochemically in the developing neural tube47. No distinct substrate or role for murine NAT3 has yet been identified. Mapping the Nat genes in mice has involved genetic linkage analysis, cloning, restriction mapping and sequencing, and cytogenetic analysis48,49. All three murine genes are within 130 kb on mouse chromosome 8 at B3.1–3.3, the orthologous region to human 8p22. Expression of murine Nat2 is under corticosterone control in adult kidney with males showing more murine NAT2 activity, and an appropriate corticosterone response element has been identified50. Initiation of transcription appears to be controlled differently in liver and kidney and at various developmental stages51. In embryonic stem (ES) cells, comparison of the sequences of murine Nat2 from cDNA and genomic DNA reveals a 6-kb non- coding exon, which must be spliced out of the transcript49. This non-coding exon has sequence homology with the non-coding exon of human NAT2. These studies suggest that murine Nat2 is the genetic equivalent of human NAT2, although the gene product is the functional equivalent of human NAT1. They also reinforce the notion that duplication of the NAT genes occurred before the divergence of mice and humans. Concluding remarks The way forward in NAT research will include the elucidation of any endogenous roles of the NATs, and identification of new functional polymorphisms in different species is likely. The elucidation of an endogenous role will probably require investigation of transgenic and knockout strains in both eukaryotic and prokaryotic organisms. It is already clear that the bacterial NATs have an endogenous role through the elimination of the rifamycin amide synthetase gene within the Ras operon of A. mediterranei. In eukaryotes, NAT is at the interface between environmental and genetic factors and in the post- genomic age, well-characterized NAT polymorphisms are likely to be a useful SNP model for analyses of multi-factorial disease aetiology. This is particularly notable in view of the location of the NAT genes in an unstable region of the human genome, which is frequently deleted and sometimes over-represented in tumours52.The probable development of transgenic mouse models will also contribute to understanding the relationship between genetic and environmental factors in causing disease. There is now substantial evidence that certain proteases, such as thrombin and trypsin, can regulate target cells by cleaving and activating a growing family of G-protein-coupled protease-activated receptors (PARs)1–8. The hallmark of this receptor family, now known to possess at least four members (PAR1–4), is the novel mechanism of receptor triggering that involves the proteolytic unmasking of a cryptic N-terminal sequence that, remaining anchored, acts as a ‘tethered’ receptor- activating ligand (Table1). For three of the PARs (i.e. PAR1, PAR2 and PAR4, but not PAR3), short synthetic peptides, based on the tethered ligand sequences, have been shown to activate the receptors and therefore mimic the effects of the activating proteases (Table1). Following the development of receptor-selective PAR-activating peptides (PAR-APs)9–11, it has been The ability of proteases to regulate cell function via protease-activated receptors (PARs) has led to new insights about the potential physiological functions of these enzymes. Several studies suggest that PARs play roles in both inflammation and tissue repair, depending on the cellular environment in which they act. The recent detection of PARs on peripheral and central neurons suggests that neuronal PARs might be involved not only in neurogenic inflammation and neurodegenerative processes, but also in nociception. Thus, the list of potential roles for PARs has lengthened considerably and their physiological course of action might be much broader than initially anticipated.
